children: Citadel is expanding its quantitative investing operation and widening its search for talent to artificial-intelligence labs as hedge funds compete with Silicon Valley for researchers, according to Bloomberg. The roughly 180-person group of financial researchers and data engineers plans to grow headcount at a "healthy" double-digit rate over the next year, said Navneet Arora, head of global quantitative strategies, and a new team led by Alexey Poyarkov — who recently joined from TGS Management — has launched to focus on systematic trading in global equities. Alongside its traditional pool of university graduates, billionaire Ken Griffin's firm is targeting researchers from AI labs such as Google DeepMind who can generate investment ideas and put increasingly powerful AI tools to work.

Even as AI automates tasks from data collection to analysis, Arora said it is not replacing human researchers but lowering the premium on coding skills while raising it on those who can generate ideas and steer machines toward profitable trades. "People can now effectively manage two, four, and in some cases even more processes. Humans are now also becoming 'managers of machines,'" he said. "Those humans, unlike machines, are not easily replaced." Citadel's Tactical Trading fund, which blends fundamental equity investing and quant strategies, is up 24.7% this year through August and has returned roughly 20% annually since its 2008 inception, a person familiar said. The firm, which manages about $76 billion across equities, fixed income and commodities, earmarks "multi-billion dollars" to quant strategies, and Arora expects the hiring to strengthen equities and build out futures and volatility strategies.

AI has widened the talent competition beyond banks and trading firms, with Citadel now vying with Silicon Valley and AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. "It's creating a new frontier for us in recruiting," said Chief Operating Officer Gerald Beeson, adding that the chance to solve complex real-world commercial problems appeals to the talent it wants. The spread of AI also raises whether shared tools will make profitable ideas quicker to exhaust — a recent New York University paper suggested a signal could lose half its excess return in about 18 months, down from five to seven years before AI. Arora argued machine learning has cut deeper into short-horizon trading, where advantages are narrow and easy to copy, than into longer-horizon strategies that rely on scarcer data and can prove more durable.

Citadel's quant group started in 2012 focused on longer-horizon strategies and has since moved into shorter-horizon trading, while high-frequency firms move the other way. "They're trying to eat each other's lunch," said James Yeh, Citadel's former chief investment officer who retired in 2021, urging heavy investment to be among the three or four players dominating the space in five years. To deter defections, Citadel is requiring non-compete agreements of up to two years for investing staff, including some analysts, and recently launched a program that pays other hedge funds for trading insights to feed its own strategies. Arora said rising fixed costs mean scale matters more than ever: "Technology, talent, everything is more expensive... I've encouraged my team to continue to think bigger and go bigger."

title: Citadel Hunts for 'Managers of Machines' in Quant Hiring Push
